passages.title: Paul measures uncertain imprisonment through the hearers' continuing need
passages.summary: Paul and Timothy write to the saints at Philippi with their overseers and servants. Paul thanks God for their partnership from the first day. He prays that their love will grow in knowledge. He says his chains have helped the good news spread through the whole guard. Some announce Christ from envy, some from good will, and he rejoices. He does not know whether he will live or die. To live is Christ, and to die is gain. He asks them to stand firm in one spirit and not fear their opponents.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Philippi as one city point. It shows no prison or home.

lds.text: Why does Paul place the hearers' need beside his own desire to depart?

contextNote.title: Paul measures uncertain imprisonment through the hearers' continuing need
contextNote.text: Paul writes in chains and does not know the outcome (verses 13 and 20). Verse 21 says both outcomes are good to him. Verse 23 states his own wish: to depart and be with Christ. Verse 24 sets the readers’ need against that wish. To remain is “more needful” for them. Verse 25 says this convinces him that he will stay. His reason for staying is their progress and joy in the faith.

passages.title: Christ's lowered position supplies the pattern for workers who serve others
passages.summary: Paul asks them to be of one mind and to do nothing from rivalry. Each should count others better than himself. He tells them to have the mind of Christ Jesus. Christ existed in the form of God and emptied himself, taking a servant’s form. He was obedient to death on a cross. God exalted him, so that every knee will bow. They are to work out their salvation and shine as lights. Paul plans to send Timothy, and he sends back Epaphroditus, who nearly died.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Philippi as one city point. It shows no prison or home.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches changed conduct through humility and care for others. How do Timothy and Epaphroditus give personal examples of concern for others?

contextNote.title: Christ's lowered position supplies the pattern for workers who serve others
contextNote.text: Verse 3 forbids rivalry and conceit. Verse 4 states the same thing as a direction for the eyes. Each is to look to the things of others, not only his own. Verses 6–8 give the pattern: Christ did not grasp equality with God. He emptied himself and became obedient to death. The chapter then names two people who do this. Timothy cares for their state (verse 20), and Epaphroditus risked his life (verse 30).

passages.title: Paul exchanges claims to rank for a pursuit he has not yet completed
passages.summary: Paul warns against those who insist on circumcision. He lists his own grounds for confidence in the flesh. He was of Benjamin, a Pharisee, and blameless in the law. He counts all of it loss for the sake of knowing Christ. He wants a righteousness that is through faith. He has not yet reached the goal and presses on toward the prize. He asks them to follow his example. He says their citizenship is in heaven, and Christ will change their bodies.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Philippi as one city point. It shows no prison or home.

lds.text: Why does Paul describe pursuit rather than claim completed perfection?

contextNote.title: Paul exchanges claims to rank for a pursuit he has not yet completed
contextNote.text: Verses 5–6 give a proud record, and verse 7 calls it loss. Verses 10–11 say what he wants: to know Christ and reach the resurrection. Verse 12 stops any claim that he has arrived. He has not obtained it and is not yet perfect. Two verbs carry the verse. Paul presses on to take hold, because Christ first took hold of him. Verse 13 repeats the denial, and verse 14 keeps him running toward the prize.

passages.title: Strength through Christ supports contentment within need and shared practical help
passages.summary: Paul begs Euodia and Syntyche to agree in the Lord. He tells them to rejoice always and to bring every request to God. God’s peace will guard their hearts. They should think on what is true, honorable, just, pure, and lovely. Paul rejoices that they have renewed their care for him. He has learned to be content in plenty and in hunger. He thanks them for the gifts sent by Epaphroditus. He sends greetings, including from those of Caesar’s household.
passages.uncertainty: The map marks Philippi as one city point. It shows no prison or home.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches joy and contentment through Christ during difficult conditions. How does the gift show that contentment can still welcome help?

contextNote.title: Strength through Christ supports contentment within need and shared practical help
contextNote.text: Verse 10 thanks the Philippians for their gift. Verse 11 at once says Paul does not speak from need. He has learned to be content in every state. Verse 12 names the states: hunger and plenty, abundance and want. “All things” in verse 13 means those conditions. Christ gives him strength to live through each one. Verse 14 still says they did well to share in his trouble.
